summary: For 10–11 year-olds dividing up to 4-digit numbers by a 2-digit divisor with formal long division, and interpreting remainders as whole numbers, fractions (remainder/divisor), decimals, or by rounding to suit context. The new demand over short division is the 2-digit divisor: the child can no longer recall facts and must estimate how many times the divisor fits at each step, so a 'menu' of the divisor's multiples (and chunking/partial-quotients) scaffolds that estimation. Estimate first, multiply back, subtract, bring down, and check by inverse multiplication.
misconceptions: Poor estimation of how many times the divisor fits, then repeated correction or errors.
Place-value errors in the quotient (dropping a place when the divisor doesn't fit).
Mishandling the remainder — wrong fraction denominator, or wrong rounding direction for the context.
Bring-down/subtraction slips propagating through the calculation.
Not checking with multiplication, so errors persist.

activities.title: Long-division workbench with a multiples menu (4752÷13)
steps: Set up 4752 ÷ 13 in the long-division layout.
Before dividing, build a side menu of multiples of 13 (13, 26, 39, 52, 65, 78, 91, 104, 117) to consult when estimating each quotient digit.

At each step, use the menu to decide how many 13s fit (e.g. 'how many 13s in 47?' → 3 because 39 ≤ 47 < 52), write that quotient digit above the correct column, multiply back, subtract, then bring down the next digit.

If the working number after bringing down is ever smaller than 13, write a 0 in the quotient for that place and bring down the next digit. This does not happen in 4752 ÷ 13 (the working numbers are 47, 85 and 72), so practise it on an example such as 3913 ÷ 13 = 301.
Finish with the remainder 7, then reframe it three ways: as the fraction 7/13 (remainder over divisor), as a decimal continuation (≈365.54), and rounded to suit a context.
Check the whole answer by computing 365×13 + 7 and confirming it equals 4752.
activities.insight: Long division by a 2-digit divisor is a repeating estimate–multiply–subtract–bring-down cycle; a multiples menu replaces the recalled facts you no longer have, and the same single division can yield several correct answers depending on how the remainder is interpreted.

activities.title: Chunking (partial quotients) as a transparent bridge
steps: Solve 4752 ÷ 13 by repeatedly subtracting easy multiples of 13: subtract 13×300 = 3900 (leaving 852), then 13×60 = 780 (leaving 72), then 13×5 = 65 (leaving 7), keeping a running tally of how many 13s you have removed.
Add the chunk counts (300 + 60 + 5 = 365) to get the quotient, with 7 left over.
Line up the chunking record beside the compact long-division layout and match each compact step to a bundled chunk.
activities.insight: The compact long-division digits are shorthand for subtracting bundles of the divisor (here 13×300, 13×60, 13×5, which give the hundreds, tens and ones digits of the quotient), so the algorithm is repeated subtraction organised by place value, not a magic routine.

activities.title: Interpreting the remainder for three contexts
steps: Take the result 4752 ÷ 13 = 365 remainder 7 and express the remainder three ways: as the fraction 7/13, as a decimal (≈0.54, giving ≈365.54), and as a rounded whole number.

Match each interpretation to a context: e.g. sharing a divisible quantity such as 4752 g of flour equally into 13 bags (fraction/decimal), versus a context where you must round up (e.g. how many buses/containers are needed), versus one where you round down (e.g. complete full groups made).
State and justify which interpretation each context demands and why rounding up or down fits.
activities.insight: One division can give several correct answers; the context decides whether the leftover is a fraction, a decimal, or forces rounding up or down.

activities.title: Check and explain each step
steps: Estimate the quotient before dividing (e.g. 13×300 = 3900 and 13×400 = 5200, so 4752÷13 is between 300 and 400; 4800÷13 ≈ 370 is a closer estimate, while 4800÷12 = 400 is a rougher overestimate) to anchor the leading digit.

After completing the division, voice what one specific step does — e.g. 'when I bring down the 5, what number am I now dividing by 13?' (answer: the brought-down value, here 85, since 47÷13 left 8 and the 5 comes down beside it).
Verify the full result by multiplying quotient×divisor and adding the remainder (365×13 + 7 = 4752).
activities.insight: Estimating first catches place-value errors, and multiplying back verifies the answer; being able to say what each step does distinguishes understanding from copying a routine.

checkQuestion: Ask the child to compute 4,752 ÷ 13 by long division while you watch, then express the remainder as a fraction. Watch how they build multiples of 13, place each quotient digit above the correct column, and carry the remainder down. Then ask them to explain what one step (e.g. 'bring down the 5') is doing.
checkAnswer: 4,752 ÷ 13 = 365 remainder 7, i.e. 365 7/13. The teacher watches for a workable long-division process (estimating how many 13s, subtracting, bringing down), correct placement of quotient digits, and expressing the remainder as 7/13 (remainder over divisor).
